canberra.title: New Birth Centre ‘like home’ as Northside Hospital design out for feedback
canberra.snippet: The proposed Northside Hospital’s Birth Centre may not be exactly what stakeholders had hoped for, but Health Infrastructure Minist...
canberra.content:
An artist’s impression of the Northside Hospital entry. Note the bush colours. Image: ACT Government.

The proposed Northside Hospital’s Birth Centre may not be exactly what stakeholders had hoped for, but Health Infrastructure Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith says mothers will feel right at home there.

The proposed Birth Centre will be part of the new hospital’s first stage – a seven-storey clinical services building at the current Bruce site.

There had been a strong push for a standalone centre, but site constraints meant a compromise, with the ground-floor Birth Centre having a separate entrance and dedicated outdoor space.

Speaking at an event on site at Bruce, marking the start of consultation on early designs for Stage 1 of the $1.5 billion hospital project, Ms Stephen-Smith stressed the proposed Birth Centre’s home-like environment and calming setting, much like that at the Townsville University Hospital she had visited.

“You wouldn’t be able to tell that you’re in a hospital building,” she said.

The centre will include dedicated access for rapid transfers to a birth suite or theatre if needed.

Health Infrastructure Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith and Health Minister Marisa Patterson at North Canberra Hospital for the launch of the new hospital consultation. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

Ms Stephen-Smith said there would be specific consultations with community members on the design.

“I’m really hoping that as people start to work through the design … that people will start to get more comfortable with what this design will look like, and more importantly, what the experience will be for women and their families and the midwives that work in that birth centre,” she said.

Beyond the Birth Centre, the new Clinical Services Building will include six birthing suites, a maternity inpatient unit and a special care nursery.

The new emergency department will include a dedicated paediatric short-stay unit, where children can be examined and treated for up to 72 hours, minimising transfers to Canberra Hospital.

The ED will also have better support for mental health presentations.

The new building will boast more than 200 new inpatient ward beds, a 14-bed intensive care unit, eight operating theatres with future-proofing for two more to be brought online when required, and two endoscopy suites with space for a third.

There will also be expanded outpatient spaces to support pre-admission clinics, specialised outpatient clinics and allied health clinics.

Where the new building will be located. Images: ACT Government.

The hospital entry.

A front view.

The Emergency Department and Ambulance Bay.

How it will sit on the campus.

The new hospital also plans to tackle the current campus’s parking issues. The present 1060 spaces are not coping, with a lot of what Ms Stephen-Smith called “informal” parking going on.

It will add 700 spaces, including 174 associated with the new early learning centre that will open towards the end of 2027.

Health Minister Marisa Patterson said the project had benefited from ongoing discussions with North Canberra Hospital staff, so it was good to see that conversation expand to the broader community.

“We’ve seen how important and beneficial the new buildings at Canberra Hospital are for staff wellbeing, for patients and for the community, and so it’s so exciting to be able to be at this stage, releasing these designs, to the community,” she said.

The early designs reveal a bush colour palette for the hospital facade, inspired by Canberra’s natural landscape, particularly the flora and fauna of Black Mountain and Bruce Ridge Nature Reserves, with references to the Gang-Gang cockatoo, eucalyptus foliage and bark.

Ms Stephen-Smith said major construction works were still due to start in 2027-28, following the opening of the new early learning centre in late 2027. Completion would be some time in 2031-32.

Once completed, the new Clinical Services Building will enable the existing Marian, Xavier and ICU buildings to be vacated.

Feedback from this consultation will inform further design work for the development application submission early next year.

To learn more, visit YourSay.

canberra.title: Mother says family kicked off Wagga bus bound for Griffith because toddler was crying
canberra.snippet: A mother has alleged a bus driver kicked her family off a long-distance coach because her 22-month-old daughter was crying, leaving the t...
canberra.content:
16 November 2026

Start the conversation

Kaneesha alleges her family was kicked off the bus because Audria was crying. Photos: Supplied.

A mother has alleged a bus driver kicked her family off a long-distance coach because her 22-month-old daughter was crying, leaving the three of them stranded on the roadside in the afternoon heat outside Wagga.

Kaneesha Williams, 30, said the family had travelled by train from Sydney to Wagga on Sunday (15 November) before boarding a connecting NSW Government coach travelling to Mildura, intending to get off at Griffith, where her grandmother was due to collect them.

In a public Facebook post, Ms Williams said the driver told her, her mother Tamara and daughter Audria to get off the coach on Coolamon Road, just outside Wagga.

The Darlington Point woman alleged the driver said he could not concentrate on driving while her daughter was crying.

She told Region her daughter was exhausted after hours of travelling, having left Sydney at 7 am, and was almost asleep when she became unsettled.

“I cannot put into words how helpless and traumatised we felt. She’s a baby. She was tired, she was crying,” Ms Williams said.

“This is the worst thing that has ever happened to me on public transport.”

She said she was doing everything she could to settle her daughter when the driver allegedly instructed them to leave about 3:15 pm.

Ms Williams said the family was left on the side of the road in the afternoon heat, without transport arrangements and with little food or water. Their mobile phone batteries were running low, and she said they had little money remaining at the end of their trip.

Kaneesha with her mother Tamara and Audria in Sydney the day before the alleged bus incident.

A Transport for NSW spokesman said he was aware of an incident involving passengers travelling on a NSW TrainLink coach service operated by Dyson between Wagga Wagga and Mildura on Sunday.

“Transport for NSW takes the concerns raised extremely seriously,” the spokesperson said.

“The operator is investigating the incident and Transport for NSW has requested updates as those enquiries progress. Passenger safety is our highest priority and we expect all operators and their employees to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism when interacting with passengers.”

Ms Williams alleges she heard the driver discussing the situation over the phone, saying he had considered allowing them back on the coach, but they would have to sit at the back and the baby would need to stop crying.

“I didn’t know how I could stop her from crying. She was really tired,” she said.

The family eventually contacted Ms Williams’ grandmother, who drove from Darlington Point to collect them after they had been left waiting for hours.

Ms Williams said other passengers did not intervene or speak up for the family.

“I just don’t want this to happen to another family,” she said.

“We were not aggressive. My baby was just so tired. She was going to fall asleep any minute.”

Ms Williams said she intended to make a formal complaint and seek legal advice.

Transport for NSW said it would update Region on its investigation as it continued.

The department has been asked whether and why the family was told to leave the coach, what circumstances justify removing passengers travelling with a young child, and whether it will be contacting the family.

More to come.

Original Article published by Oliver Jacques on Region Riverina.

canberra.title: Helen Haines discharged from hospital, describing it as ‘really positive moment’
canberra.snippet: Independent MP Helen Haines has been released from hospital, a month after she was rammed by a car outside her electorate office in Wanga...
canberra.content:
Independent Member for Indi Helen Haines has thanked her carers and well-wishers in a statement on her release from hospital. Photo: George Tsotsos.

Independent MP Helen Haines has been released from hospital, a month after she was rammed by a car outside her electorate office in Wangaratta on 19 October.

The Member for Indi, who lost both her legs as a result of the incident, described her release as a “really positive moment” and thanked her carers and well-wishers.

Dr Haines was in the Alfred Hospital and will remain in Melbourne for the time being to undergo rehabilitation therapy.

“I am very pleased to confirm that I have moved into the rehabilitation stage of my recovery, which will continue in Melbourne for the immediate future,” she said in a statement issued on Monday (16 November), exactly four weeks since she was struck by the vehicle.

“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred and am receiving in this next stage.

“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world.

“They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing.

“I am overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians in the form of donations to Save the Children, and I look forward to working with them in due course on applying these funds to improve the lives of children.”

Dr Haines’ husband, Phil Haines, had asked the public on her behalf to donate to Save the Children in lieu of flowers, and so far the charity has raised more than $1.46 million through Haines’s fundraising appeal.

Anthony Albanese also issued a statement on Monday to wish Dr Haines well: “All our thoughts and prayers continue to be with Helen for her recovery.

“I have been in regular contact with Helen and her extraordinary family.

“We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation.”

Other federal parliamentarians, when appearing at press conferences in Parliament House on other matters, also took the opportunity to wish the independent MP a good recovery.

Health Minister Mark Butler said he welcomed the news of Dr Haines’ discharge from hospital.

“I think all of us welcome every milestone in Helen’s recovery as wonderful news,” he said.

“We know these are devastating injuries, though, and her road to recovery is going to be a long one.

“But each of these milestones that we’ve heard over recent weeks have been so warmly welcomed by everyone in this building, and people in the broader community as well.

“And we wish her and her family all the best.”

Greens leader David Shoebridge also mentioned Dr Haines when speaking to the media.

“It’s extraordinary to think about just what her journey has been on these last weeks,” Senator Shoebridge said.

“We just wish her every possible recovery; and the fact that she could be out of hospital, surrounded by a community, surrounded by her family, I hope that helps with her healing.”

Police have charged Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, 43, with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally causing serious injury and the Commonwealth offence of causing harm to a Commonwealth public official.

They will allege Dr Haines was standing by the boot of her car outside her electoral office when Nugent did a U-turn in his car and struck her repeatedly.

Nugent has also been charged with two additional offences of cultivating and possessing cannabis.

The accused is known to Dr Haines and her family.

The 65-year-old Member for Indi has been granted a leave of absence from Federal Parliament for the rest of the year.

She remained in a critical condition in hospital from the time of the attack until 24 October, when her condition was downgraded to serious but stable.

canberra.title: Illegal tobacco volume drops following coordinated enforcement crackdown
canberra.snippet: There has been a dramatic fall in the volume of illicit tobacco products in Australia due to targeted border control measures and a conce...
canberra.content:
Coordinated enforcement measures at borders and across the country have put a dent in the illicit tobacco trade. Photo: Australian Federal Police.

There has been a dramatic fall in the volume of illicit tobacco products in Australia due to targeted border control measures and a concerted, cross-jurisdictional crackdown on the sale of illegal cigarettes and vapes.

The Federal Government is celebrating new figures from the Illicit Tobacco and E-cigarette (ITEC) Commissioner, released on Monday (16 November), which show the illicit tobacco market in Australia is now smaller than it was last year.

The total volume of the illicit tobacco market has shrunk by between 79 tonnes and 1438 tonnes from last year’s peak estimate, representing as much as a 24 per cent reduction in volume.

ITEC estimates black market tobacco has dropped to 5893 tonnes, but could even be as low as 4453 tonnes.

It says an exact figure is all but impossible to determine because of the market’s illegal nature, but databases from several sources, including the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, have produced an accurate, narrow range.

The drop in illicit tobacco products reverses the average annual growth in volume of 22.6 per cent seen over the previous five years.

Last financial year, Australian Border Force seized more than 2300 tonnes of illicit tobacco and 13.2 million vaping devices.

Domestic enforcement led to a 496 per cent increase in cigarette stick seizures, and a 232 per cent increase in loose-leaf tobacco seizures, compared to the domestic seizures in the previous financial year.

Assistant Minister for Customs, Julian Hill, said the good news is due to stronger enforcement measures, larger seizures and greater coordination between jurisdictions.

“Just 12 months into scaled-up enforcement via the Australian Border Force-led National Disruption Group, the data is encouraging, including record seizures at the border,” he said.

“We’re investing close to $100 million to support states and territories with street-level enforcement and dialling up shop closures.

“This builds on the success in South Australia and Queensland where crackdowns have seen legal sales rise and more smokers call the Quitline.

“As other states and territories follow South Australia’s and Queensland’s lead and dial up shop closures, we want to see a bigger impact on the illicit market.”

ABF seized more than 730 tonnes of illicit tobacco in the first quarter of this financial year, which was an all-time high and a 50 per cent increase on the same time last year.

The seizures included more than 3.75 million vapes, an 18 per cent increase compared to the first quarter last financial year.

The National Disruption Group is actively coordinating 31 federal, state and territory partners, including the Australian Federal Police, state and territory police forces, Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission, Therapeutic Goods Administration, and AUSTRAC.

In its first year, it coordinated more than 600 enforcement actions against 486 targets nationwide, resulting in the seizure of more than 24 million illicit cigarettes, 3.6 tonnes of loose-leaf tobacco, 356,000 vapes and $2.4 million in cash, representing more than $45 million in evaded tobacco duty.

Over the past 12 months, NDG activities have led to the identification of 354 persons of interest, 195 partner referrals and 32 visa cancellation referrals and have contributed to the closure of 63 illicit tobacco premises across Australia.

Across the country, states and territories are ramping up on-the-ground action, with more than 1300 store closures nationwide.

International cooperation is also playing a critical role in Australia’s crackdown on illicit tobacco, with 340 referrals from foreign partners contributing to the seizure of 216.7 tonnes of tobacco and 832,500 vapes in the most recent quarter.

That’s a 95 per cent increase in volume compared to last year.

But the Assistant Minister said the government would not be releasing Treasury modelling showing the relationship between the hike in the tobacco excise and rising smoking rates.

The Coalition and One Nation have both announced policies to treat the illicit tobacco as a public health issue and slash the tobacco excise by 80 per cent and 75 per cent, respectively.

That would crush the illegal trade, they have each stated, but Labor has rejected the idea, saying law enforcement is the best way to tackle the problem.

“Every illicit cigarette seized, every store closed and every network disrupted sends the same message to criminals – we know who you are, we know how you operate, and we’re coming after you and your profits,” Mr Hill said.

“Now is the time to double down, not back down, as the Coalition and One Nation want to do by letting vapes rip – risking young Australians getting hooked on nicotine and condemned to smoking-related diseases and early death.

“The Albanese Government will not surrender our nation’s health policy to organised crime…

“We’re very clear from looking at the international evidence through the work of the Tobacco Commissioner, that these organised criminal syndicates are attacking countries, regardless of public health policies,” Mr Hill said.

canberra.title: The tiny Snowy Mountains fish that got a second chance after Black Summer
canberra.snippet: The Dunns Road fire was still burning in January 2020 when NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) firefighters escorted a fish re...
canberra.content:
Charles Sturt University fish ecologist Dr Amina Price examines 10 healthy adult stocky galaxias recaptured in a Snowy Mountains stream after being bred in captivity and released into the wild. Photo: Snowy Hydro.

The Dunns Road fire was still burning in January 2020 when NSW National Parks and Wildlife Service (NPWS) firefighters escorted a fish rescue team into Kosciuszko National Park (KNP).

Heavy rain was forecast, and if it washed ash and sediment into Tantangara Creek, it could choke the only stretch of water where the critically endangered stocky galaxias was then known to live.

The team caught 142 of the finger-length fish and took them to the Gaden Trout Hatchery near Jindabyne.

The rescue bought time for a species scientists had formally described only six years earlier and helped start a breeding program at Charles Sturt University’s Gulbali Institute in Albury.

NSW Fisheries researchers have now recaptured 10 healthy adult stocky galaxias in a Snowy Mountains stream where they had previously released fish bred in Albury.

Usually just 7.5 to 8.5 centimetres long, the stocky galaxias has no scales, a blunt snout and gold eyes, with dark flecks across its olive-brown head and back.

Its broad body gives the fish its common name, while its scientific name, Galaxias tantangara, comes from the creek where the first specimens were collected.

A second natural population has since been confirmed in Sallys Flat Creek, also in KNP.

In both creeks, the fish live in cold, clear water that averages just 10 to 30 centimetres deep, with shelter beneath the banks and among rocks or vegetation.

They live above waterfalls that keep out introduced brown and rainbow trout, which prey on them.

With both populations confined to short stretches of creek, severe drought can shrink their habitat, while erosion along the banks can wash soil into the shallow water.

In a refrigerated shipping container fitted out as a lab at Charles Sturt University’s Thurgoona campus, freshwater fish ecologist Dr Amina Price and her team spent several years working out how to get the stocky galaxias to breed in captivity.

They adjusted water temperatures and hours of light to mimic the seasons in an alpine creek, and by early 2023 the first fish had hatched in captivity.

“No one had ever bred stocky galaxias in captivity before,” Gulbali Institute executive director Lee Baumgartner said.

That April, university researchers and NSW Fisheries staff released about 130 stocky galaxias at Eucumbene Borrows, a former Snowy Mountains Hydro Scheme site they hoped could support a third population.

Among them were six adult males rescued from Tantangara Creek during Black Summer.

The team released another 243 lab-bred fish at the site in May 2024, but few turned up in follow-up surveys.

Monitoring suggested the water could get too warm in summer, and further releases at Eucumbene Borrows were put on hold.

Snowy Hydro says researchers have since released about 250 young stocky galaxias into alpine streams, the biggest release so far.

The 10 adults came from an earlier release at an undisclosed location.

“To achieve a world first, then take those fish and put them back into the wild and see the wild population grow … it’s incredible,” Professor Baumgartner said.

NSW Fisheries runs the breeding program with funding from Snowy Hydro under the Snowy 2.0 fish management plan, which sets out how the company will protect threatened native fish from risks posed by the project, including the spread of fish between waterways.

Pumping water from Talbingo Reservoir to Tantangara Reservoir could carry another fish with it, the climbing galaxias, which is native to coastal rivers in eastern Australia.

From Tantangara Reservoir, it could move up the creek and get past the natural waterfall.

If it reached the headwaters, it could eat stocky galaxias and compete with them for food.

Snowy Hydro finished building a barrier above the falls in May 2025 to keep the climbing galaxias out, as required under the project’s NSW approval.

The next test is whether the released fish can breed there and establish a population that survives without further releases.

“Our aim is to establish several secure, self-sustaining populations across the landscape, so the species is better protected if bushfire, invasive species or another disturbance affects one location,” Dr Price said.

Original Article published by Edwina Mason on About Regional.

australia.title: Proposed NSW laws to allow coalmine to increase production pose ‘serious corruption risk’
australia.snippet: Bill to authorise expansion at Mount Pleasant coalmine, subject to a landmark high court decision, will be debated this week Get our dail...
australia.content:
A New South Wales government bill to increase coal production at a Hunter Valley coalmine creates a “serious corruption risk” for the state due to a clause that would give the resources minister “king-like” powers, the barrister and anti-corruption campaigner Geoffrey Watson says.

The state parliament will this week debate legislation to allow MACH Energy to increase coal production at the Mount Pleasant mine in Muswellbrook by 32% to 16.5m tonnes per year.

The Minns government announced the bill last month after the high court ruled that an expansion of the mine was invalidly approved. The government has said the legislation is necessary to prevent 400 job losses at the site before Christmas.

Watson, the Greens and some members of the crossbench have raised concerns that a clause in the bill would give the resources minister of the day “unusually broad” powers to override other state laws.

Known as a Henry VIII clause, it would allow the minister to make regulations that could modify laws of the state as they apply to the Mount Pleasant development.

Henry VIII provisions are sometimes used by parliaments and draw their name from King Henry VIII and his style of governing by royal proclamation.

Watson is a director of the Centre for Public Integrity and Grata Fund and a former counsel assisting the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac).

In a legal analysis of the bill, he raised concerns that Clause 17 “explicitly places” wide powers to “make new laws (or to repeal or modify existing laws) in the hands of one person – the mining minister – and for a single coal mine owner”.

“There are real problems with this as it is known that the concentration of this kind of power in the hands of one person creates a serious corruption risk,” he wrote.

He said the risk was “heightened” because the Mount Pleasant bill had been created for a single private company. He wrote that while he imputed “no bad faith at all to the current mining minister”, past experience in the state “has shown that not all ministers have acted in a manner free from improper motives”.

“Historically, we’ve seen this concentration of power into the hands of a single decision maker as posing a serious risk of corruption,” Watson told Guardian Australia.

“Now, corruption in that sense may not mean money passing hands. It also includes undue influence, decisions made in [circumstances] other than the public interest.”

Elaine Johnson is the director of Johnson Legal, which represented the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg) in the high court proceedings. In a separate legal opinion, she raised similar concerns there was “a very obvious corruption risk arising from Clause 17”.

She wrote that the clause gave the resources minister of the day “unfettered power to make regulations to change the application of any law of the state” to the mine, and said it could potentially affect many laws that applied to the mine, such as those that regulate noise and dust or worker safety.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

The lower house is expected to debate the legislation on Tuesday, followed by the upper house later this week. The Minns government is hoping to pass the bill in what is likely to be the final sitting week before the March 2027 election.

Both Labor and Coalition lower house seats are under pressure from One Nation in the Hunter, where the mine is located.

One Nation’s NSW leader and candidate for Cessnock, Mike Newman, has described the Minns government’s bill to increase production limits at Mount Pleasant as a “Band-Aid on a bullet-wound”.

The Coalition resources spokesperson and Nationals MP for Upper Hunter, Dave Layzell, said the opposition would not oppose Labor’s legislation “in any way”. Asked about the Henry VIII clause, he said the Coalition would follow advice on the bill from the parliament’s legislation review committee which is expected on Tuesday.

“We recognise [Labor’s] argument about the need to protect the number of jobs they are quoting.

“We agree that it is important that we fix the situation with the Mount Pleasant Mine extension.

“We cannot allow green environmental lawfare to continue to delay projects that have the support of the majority of the community, and are approved on a technical basis by the planning system.”

The Greens climate spokesperson Sue Higginson said it was “the broadest” Henry VIII clause she had seen during the current parliament and the party would seek to remove it from the bill or limit its scope.

“Placing that much power in the hands of a single minister is a corruption risk the Labor government should know well,” she said.

“A tightly limited Henry VIII provision can be necessary to give effect to parliament’s decision over time, as with the recent Great Koala National Park bill, where it allowed more land to be permanently protected in the public interest as it becomes available.”

A spokesperson for the resources minister, Courtney Houssos, said the government had been clear that the purpose of its bill was to protect all permanent workers at Mount Pleasant. They said the bill had been presented transparently to parliament.

“We welcome constructive engagement on the Bill from crossbenchers and will engage with good-faith amendments as we always do,” they said.

“Any proposed regulation would be submitted to the Executive Council for approval and published transparently in the usual manner, and also subject to disallowance in the usual manner.”

They added that Henry VIII provisions had been “routinely” used in legislation for decades, including in bills the Greens had supported in this term of parliament.

The independent MP Alex Greenwich, who intends to oppose the bill as a whole, said the provision was “dangerously broad and quite unprecedented”.

“It’s especially concerning, given parliament won’t sit for six months, meaning regulations issued during that time won’t be able to be disallowed,” he said.

australia.title: Pay $8,000 or go uninsured: premiums far outpace inflation, putting many Australians in an impossible position
australia.snippet: Insurance premiums have increased by nearly 50% in five years, turning basic coverage into an unaffordable luxury for some Get our breaki...
australia.content:
The cost of home insurance has surged at twice the pace of inflation over the past five years, leaving homeowners like Matthew with an impossible choice: pay up to $8,000 a year for a policy or go uninsured.

For Matthew, who lives in regional Victoria and asked to be identified by his first name only, skyrocketing premiums have turned basic coverage into an unaffordable luxury, especially after his insurer denied a previous claim and cancelled his policy.

“Because I have both a cancellation and a claim history, I’m looking at anywhere between $6,000 to $8,000 for a policy with full coverage, which I simply can’t afford,” he says. “In any other industry, it would be called fraud.”

For homeowners like Matthew, whose claim history or exposure to natural disasters puts them in the highest-risk brackets, premium hikes are particularly punishing. Yet the surge is hitting the entire market.

Guardian analysis shows the overall cost of insurance has increased by twice as much as the cost of living over the past five years. Overall inflation has climbed by 23% since December 2021 and insurance premiums surged by 46% over the same period.

While the insurance industry says the rising cost of goods and services is a key reason it needs to increase premium prices for customers, inflation and corresponding cost-of-living struggles mean some customers are downgrading their coverage or forgoing insurance altogether.

High insurance premiums aren’t just straining household budgets, they are actively fuelling inflation and keeping upward pressure on interest rates. Yet while politicians routinely scrutinise grocery and power bills, insurance costs rarely attract the same attention.

“On the one hand, inflation pushes up insurance costs,” says Associate Prof Fei Huang, from the University of New South Wales business school. “On the other … rising insurance prices also contribute directly to measured inflation.”

Huang says people may be dropping their coverage to reduce the pressure on their budgets, even if being underinsured put them in a vulnerable long-term position.

She says insurers across all industries should be more transparent, pointing to a recent Asic review of car insurers that found none explained to customers how they calculated premiums, affecting their ability to shop around.

“Customers may face increasing insurance prices, but not understand why the prices are increasing or what actions can they take to reduce the price,” Huang says.

Big profits despite increased costs

The Insurance Council of Australia (ICA) says it supports giving consumers clear information about premium changes and has been engaging with the federal government on pricing transparency reforms.

“However, transparency will not reduce premiums because it does not change the risk a home faces or what it costs to repair or rebuild,” an ICA spokesperson says.

The ICA says higher insurance premiums are “a result of inflation, not the cause of it”, with increases in building costs, extreme weather and state-based taxes being some of the main drivers.

“The only sustainable path to lower premiums is investment in climate risk mitigation, stronger homes and better land-use planning,” it says.

Sally Tindall, the data insights director at financial comparison website Canstar, says the inflation of medical costs, electricity and business expenses are also contributing to increased premiums, along with the increased frequency of natural disasters.

In August, the Suncorp chief executive officer, Steve Johnston, said his insurance company had exceeded its $1.77bn budget for “natural hazards” by $254m in the 2025-26 financial year, and paid out more than $10bn in claims.

Nevertheless, insurance companies are making a lot of money. Suncorp reported a net profit after tax of $1.03bn in the last financial year. It and the other big publicly listed insurers have fared better than the broader share market.

Shares in Suncorp, which owns AAMI and Apia, have risen by 17.11% this year. Over the same period, shares in the Sydney-headquartered multinational insurer QBE – which made US$2.13bn (A$3.01bn) in net profit in 2025 – have lifted by 35.14%.

Shares in IAG, which describes itself as Australia’s largest general insurer and owns NRMA among other brands, have jumped by 14.29%. In the 12 months to June, the company recorded a $1.02bn net profit after tax. By comparison, the benchmark ASX 200 has risen by a modest 3.99% this year.

At the same time, on average, insurance policies have become more expensive. Home insurance premiums alone have increased by more than 50% on average in the past five years across Australia, according to the consumer group Choice.

IAG, QBE and Suncorp say they recognise Australians are under cost-of-living pressures.

An IAG spokesperson says it offers support for customers facing financial vulnerability, but a “financially strong and sustainable insurance sector plays a critical role in helping individuals and businesses manage the risks they face, including the rising impacts of extreme weather”.

A spokesperson for Suncorp says it remains focused on “disciplined pricing and efficient claims management”, adding governments should “reduce insurance taxes and invest in resilience” to reduce the underlying risk.

A QBE spokesperson says improving insurance affordability requires “insurers, governments, industries, and communities to work together” and should include greater investment in disaster resilience.

People reducing coverage to cope

Tyrone Shandiman, the chair of the Australian Consumers Insurance Lobby, says that price increases have peaked, and premiums should start to come down or at least increase more in line with inflation.

Across Australia, average home insurance premiums for new policies increased by $101, or 4%, from 2025 to 2026, according to Canstar. Average comprehensive car insurance premiums increased by $111, or 5%. Despite these increases returning near the rate of inflation, they come on top of previous large increases and the cost is not going backwards.

The insurance consultancy Finity says that while industry-wide premium growth has slowed, premiums are not necessarily falling.

Shandiman acknowledges there are people who can’t afford insurance, and who are choosing to forgo it for other expenses.

“If you’ve got to choose between putting food on the table and insuring your house … people are going to choose putting food on the table,” he says.

Brendan Ross, a senior policy officer at the Consumer Action Law Centre, says insurance is becoming even more unaffordable and difficult to access in certain areas due to climate change, and the associated increased risk of natural disasters.

“If you’re underinsured and something happens, you’re not covered for it basically – that’s when that stress and potential consumer harm really becomes prevalent,” he says. “That can have a real impact on people.”

Ross points to modelling by the insurance regulator Apra which estimated one in four households would be underinsured by 2050, up from one in seven households in 2026.

Canstar research has found people are already reducing their coverage to cope with the expense. While more people hold health insurance, for example, there are fewer people with top-tier coverage.

In February, when Canstar surveyed 2,254 privately insured Australians, 17% said they planned to reduce or remove their extras cover, 13% planned to remove or reduce their hospital cover, and 13% planned to downgrade their level of coverage.

Almost two years ago, a parliamentary inquiry into the impact of climate change on insurance premiums recommended insurance companies be forced to disclose insurance premium calculations amid a surge in the cost of household policies.

The inquiry, which was chaired by the Greens, heard from people all over the country who raised concerns about the rising cost of insurance premiums. The government is yet to respond to the report.

The Greens want the government to mandate transparency around how premiums are calculated, with the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission monitoring and publicly reporting on insurance prices.

In the meantime, Matthew remains sceptical of insurers’ claims after his home in Kerang, a town in northern Victoria, was flooded in December 2023. He says the disaster has left him with a damage bill of $150,000 and no help from his insurer.

He is dubious that insurance companies need to increase their premiums by so much because of inflation.

“If you increase a policy or a premium by 20% or 30% or 40%, you are creating the inflation,” he says. “You’re not increasing because of it. You are the cause of it.”

australia.title: ‘Aboriginal people were the backbone of this state’: rediscovered photographs reveal life inside the 1946 Pilbara strike camps
australia.snippet: Eighty years after hundreds of Aboriginal workers walked off Pilbara stations, a trove of photos found beneath a wardrobe documents what ...
australia.content:
Troy Eaton lives in Pippingarra, near Port Hedland, where the Pilbara’s multibillion-dollar mining industry looms large. “It’s a mecca of mining,” says the Nyamal man. But his family’s mining history stretches back long before the arrival of today’s resources giants.

In September, Eaton took the long drive from Pippingarra to Perth to see some of those early pioneers: his ancestors, who established their own mining ventures in the Pilbara some 80 years ago.

On the walls of Lawrence Wilson Art Gallery at the University of Western Australia (UWA), he saw colour photographs of women sifting minerals with shallow tin yandies, and men wielding picks and shovels beneath vast blue skies. Among them were his grandmother, Kakaya Lucy Mitchell, his great-grandmother and other relatives, captured in photographs he had never seen. “It’s a bit emotional … just reminiscing on what it was like in their time,” he says.

“They look healthy. They look happy. There was a sense of pride looking at it, because they was doing something that they could never believe, most probably in their lifetime – taking control of their own destiny.”

The photographs feature in Strike Camps: The Photographs of John Wilson, an exhibition documenting the independent mining communities established after the 1946 Pilbara strike, when about 800 Aboriginal workers walked off pastoral stations over appalling conditions and meagre wages. Many were paid only in rations of tea, flour, sugar and tobacco.

The walk-off soon became more than a labour dispute. Hundreds of workers established camps near Port Hedland and Marble Bar, building spinifex shelters and setting up schools. Over the following years, they supported themselves by mining tin, beryl and other minerals, as well as pearl shelling and collecting buffel grass seed.

The camps offered them a measure of freedom from pastoralists’ control and the chance to raise families on their own terms. In 1952, their mining company, Northern Development and Mining, produced minerals worth £70,000.

The anthropologist John Wilson photographed the camps in the late 1950s and early 1960s, conducting fieldwork alongside his wife and fellow anthropologist, Katrin. Both have since died, and this year their daughter Bu unearthed a cache of slides beneath a wardrobe in the family’s Fremantle home, helping reunite an archive of some 350 colour images.

The UWA art historian Darren Jorgensen, who co-curated the exhibition, had spent years searching for Wilson’s photographs. They form what he calls “the most substantial collection of pictures” of the camps, documenting Aboriginal self-determination 20 years before the Gurindji walk-off at Wave Hill, the 1966 strike that became a turning point in Australia’s land rights movement.

Jorgensen believes the Pilbara strike remains less well known partly because it lacked a defining image, unlike Wave Hill’s famous photograph of Gough Whitlam pouring soil into Vincent Lingiari’s hand. Yet the communities Wilson photographed had achieved something remarkable: at a time when Aboriginal people in Western Australia were still denied the vote and subjected to discriminatory laws, “they were making international mining deals and shipping off barrels of columbite to Singapore,” he says.

Alongside 35 photographs, the exhibition features two short films that use generative AI to animate scenes of work and everyday life in the Pilbara camps. Created by the exhibition co-curator and UWA fine arts head, Vladimir Todorović, the films were developed in consultation with descendants of the strikers.

The strike itself was carefully orchestrated. As early as March 1945, more than a year before the walk-off, Nyamal organiser Clancy McKenna and Nyangumarta lawman Dooley Binbin travelled between remote pastoral stations, distributing makeshift calendars drawn on food packaging, including jam-tin labels, so workers could count down to the planned walk-off on 1 May. With the help of white prospector Don McLeod, they coordinated a strike that spread across more than 20 stations and some 10,000 square kilometres. Both Aboriginal leaders were jailed, but the strike gathered strength.

The walk-off lasted three years, making it the longest recorded strike in Australian history. But the workers’ right to remain in their camps was contested. In 1949, when authorities ordered families to dismantle their homes at Twelve Mile, near Port Hedland, the strikers protested in writing, warning that the closure could reignite the dispute. The government subsequently withdrew the order. The strike ended that year with improved pay and conditions at two stations but unfulfilled promises of wider reform. Some returned to work on sheep and cattle stations; others stayed in the communities they had built, which endured for decades.

Eaton’s grandfather Putangaja Ernie Mitchell became a key leader, coordinating mining operations and negotiating with government officials. Mitchell’s daughter Doris, who also attended the exhibition opening, remembers growing up in the camps, where children sifted ore and traded tins of minerals for lollies. Welfare authorities once labelled her a “neglected child”. “But I wasn’t neglected,” she says. “As children, we grew up with many parents.”

Yet even within the mining cooperatives, control remained contested. In 1959, Mitchell and fellow leader Peter Kangkushot Coppin broke with McLeod amid disagreements over how earnings were used, with workers receiving rations rather than cash. Wilson photographed a meeting as the movement split. “They didn’t get any money in their hands,” Doris recalls.

Mitchell and Coppin continued the mining cooperative known as Pindan, while McLeod’s supporters formed another, Nomads. Both groups went on to establish pastoral enterprises: Pindan’s successors at Yandeyarra and Nomads at Strelley, where an independent Aboriginal school established in 1976 still operates today.

One of the last surviving strikers, Nyamal elder Captain Mudjawariny Wilson, is now in his 90s and living in aged care in Roebourne. His daughter Ursula, an exhibition co-curator, brought him to Perth for the exhibition’s opening, where he recognised himself working as a young man in the photographs. “When I first looked at the pictures, I stood there and had tears in my eyes,” Ursula recalls.

For Eaton, the photographs tell a story too often overlooked. “We always hear doom and gloom stories, but we don’t hear any great stories like this,” he says. This year, he notes, Rio Tinto celebrated 60 years of Pilbara operations; his ancestors were mining there decades earlier. “Aboriginal people were actually the backbone of this state.”

Eighty years after the strike began, Eaton is working to establish an Aboriginal-owned mining venture in the Pilbara, pursuing the same independence his grandfather’s generation fought for.

“I need to finish that journey,” he says. “Because my grandfather and those guys started it back then, right? And that journey continues to this day.”

australia.title: Birth keeper told mother of baby who later died to ‘go home and rest’, NSW inquest hears
australia.snippet: Sita Kali was involved in care for two of four babies who died between 2022 and 2024 in Lismore after free births or home births Get our ...
australia.content:
A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.

Sita Tara Kali was involved in the care of two of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. An inquest into the deaths began in the Lismore local court on Monday. The families of the four babies were not present.

The inquest will examine whether the care was reasonable in the circumstances and whether care by an unregistered support worker was reasonable and appropriate before, during and after the birth.

Baby R’s mother had a distrust of hospitals in general, the court heard. She was aligned with and trusted Kali. She felt that having a home birth would give her a stronger connection to the baby. In a police statement she said she felt threatened by her experiences at the hospital.

At 43 weeks, an ultrasound confirmed that the baby was extremely compromised. The obstetric advice was urgent. She was urged to attend emergency and strongly advised against a home birth, the inquest heard.

She called Kali, who said in a police statement, “she was quite upset and anxious. I advised her to go home and rest. Calm yourself down and consider what you want to do.”

Baby R was born outside into his father’s hands at 9.51am. Two doulas were in attendance; neither had medical training. The baby was white in colour. He never latched on to feed.

About 14 hours later, the ambulance was called. The umbilical cord and placenta were still attached. Baby R died on the way to a waiting helicopter at 12.22am.

The cause of his death was determined to be unascertained. But an expert neonatologist surmised that it was caused by hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy resulting from severe post-maturity – being born at 43 weeks.

Prof Hannah Dahlen, a midwifery academic who has attended thousands of births, told the court that this was a baby “I would have been watching closely” as a midwife attending a birth.

She said the difference between a doula and a birthing midwife “is the theoretical knowledge that we add on to that clinical experience, which gives us an understanding and an ability to interpret signs and symptoms and to identify what pathology is going on, or what physiology is not actually working at this time and making a decision”.

The counsel assisting, Ragni Mathur, told the court women were choosing unregulated free birthing because of “traumatic or coercive experiences, fragmented care, lack of trust in clinicians, lack of available clinicians, lack of services in regional NSW, and including child protection notifications and regulatory actions against new lives”.

australia.title: Albanese treads tightrope in upcoming Trump meeting, wanting Indo-Pacific engagement and end to Iran and Ukraine wars
australia.snippet: Quad leaders’ summit in Philippines is Trump’s first, as Australia joins US and Japan to protect AI technologies in face of China efforts...
australia.content:
Anthony Albanese will attempt to walk a tightrope in his relationship with Donald Trump when the pair meets on Tuesday, arguing for a speedy resolution to the wars in Iran and Ukraine while urging the US to engage in the Indo-Pacific.

The Quad leaders’ summit in the Philippines’ capital of Manila will be Trump’s first, in either of his presidencies. The US president, fresh from a crushing midterms result, will take centre stage in gatherings of Asian leaders and prepare for historic three-way talks with Xi Jinping of China and Russia’s Vladimir Putin this week.

Underlying the diplomatic swing are efforts by the federal government to avoid angering China, as the Quad leaders gather for the first time since 2024 – and after Australia joined countries, including the US and Japan, in an agreement for new protections around key AI technologies.

Designed to firm up supply chains for chips and critical minerals components, the San Francisco Declaration was crafted to promote cooperation in the face of China’s efforts to control areas of AI development.

Part of the Pax Silica international accord, officials said the agreement would help ensure Trump worked with partners to set standards in AI, rather than relying on others for leadership. Signatories include the UK, India, Israel, South Korea and Singapore.

  • Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter here

Albanese told the Asean-Australia summit on Monday that the region needed friendship, mutual trust, and optimism to prosper.

“At a time of global instability, the cooperation we demonstrate here will help us to confront the challenges we share at home and in our region,” he said.

Federal government sources told Guardian Australia the intense international efforts, including Albanese’s attendance at the Apec leaders’ meeting in Shenzhen, China at the end of the week, was about maintaining engagement with Trump in the final two years of his presidency and stopping the US from withdrawing from global leadership.

Asia Society senior fellow Premesha Saha said the Quad talks would focus on critical minerals, maritime security and energy security.

“For Australia, keeping the United States engaged in the Indo-Pacific is a core strategic interest, and the Quad is one of the few settings where the president is tied into a regional agenda alongside three close partners,” Saha said.

“After a year in which Washington has been engaged elsewhere and has opened its own channel with Beijing, getting Trump to a Quad leaders’ meeting in the region matters to Australia.”

Saha said Albanese’s objectives included keeping Washington engaged in the region and building a Quad capable of delivering results, even during shifts in US policy and interest.

“Beijing will criticise it, as it always does, and will cast it as bloc politics. But I will be cautious about overstating how much this will anger China,” she said.

“The Quad isn’t a military alliance, and Washington has gone out of its way to say it isn’t an anti-China coalition.”

Jennifer Parker, a non-resident fellow at the Lowy Institute, said criticism of Albanese’s involvement in the annual international summit season was shortsighted.

“Our relationships in the region are essential to our security in an increasingly chaotic world, and our security is the backbone of our national prosperity,” she said.

“It is important for Australia to be seen on the international stage and advocate for our national interests.”

Parker disagreed that Australia was working to keep the US engaged in the Asia Pacific region.

“The US has enduring interests here, both economically and strategically. But sometimes it pays for Australia to remind them of that,” she said.

Albanese announced a new Asean-Australia digital economy program on Monday, to support AI safety and intelligence standards and digital trade standards.

He said humans must remain in control of AI, shaping the technology “rather than let it shape us”.

Albanese also held one-on-one talks with the Philippines president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

He told his Laos counterpart, Saleumxay Kommasith, that Australia remained very concerned about the deaths of backpackers Bianca Jones and Holly Morton-Bowles, who died after drinking methanol-laced alcohol at a hostel in Vientiane in 2024.

Albanese said Australia remained concerned about the seriousness of charges over the deaths. Investigators said they did not have enough evidence to do more because autopsies were not carried out.

Albanese called the case a “tragedy” and said it remained a serious issue in Australia.

Kommasith said the Laos government had attached importance to the case and officials were “trying our best to put an end to this by bringing those perpetrators into justice”.

world.title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda
world.snippet: Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’ Five EU member ...
world.content:
Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

In a statement released on Monday the five EU countries said “concrete negotiations with partner country Rwanda will begin for implementation”, saying the scheme would make “an important contribution to further curbing illegal migration, dismantling the business model of smugglers and relieving the burden on our population”.

Officials hope to send 100 people to Rwanda from early next year to test the model. The scheme will apply to adults whose claims to asylum have been rejected or others with no legal right to live in the EU.

In theory, according to diplomatic sources, migrants would stay in a reception centre in Rwanda for a couple of months, before choosing to integrate into life in the Great Lakes country or return to their home nation.

Unlike the failed scheme pursued by the British Conservative government in Rwanda, or Italy’s agreement with Albania, it will not apply to people pursuing asylum claims.

The reception centre, which would be an open facility, was not intended to house people long term but to accommodate regular flows of people, the countries said. Diplomatic sources said the EU countries were not using British-funded facilities built in Kigali.

The governments involved argue it will protect the European asylum system while removing the incentive for irregular migrants to come to Europe.

Denmark’s immigration minister, Morten Bødskov, whose government has pioneered a tough line on migration widely emulated across the EU, said it was “a huge breakthrough”.

The German interior minister, Alexander Dobrindt, said: “Return hubs offer a positive approach for people without the right to stay and with no prospects in Europe, whose countries of origin do not cooperate in the repatriation process.”

Andy Burnham told reporters last week that the UK had not had direct discussions with European governments involved in return hubs but “we will watch that with interest, learning from what went on in the past. The public want us to do whatever we can to deal with illegal immigration.”

Critics have highlighted the ethical difficulties of striking an agreement with Rwanda’s repressive government, which was found in 2024 by the US state department to allow state security forces and civilian officials to commit human rights abuses with impunity, while also raising concerns about freedom of expression and forced labour.

The French Green MEP Mélissa Camara denounced the agreement between the five countries and Rwanda as “an agreement of shame” and “a grave moral failing”. She said: “Under this agreement, people will be deported thousands of kilometres away from the European Union, with no guarantees regarding the compliance with their rights.”

Alain Berset, the secretary general of the Council of Europe, the continent’s human rights body, said it was not possible “to be so precise a priori” about what any return hubs proposal meant. Speaking to the Guardian before the announcement, he said all members of the Council of Europe were committed to the European convention on human rights “and this must be the lighthouse” for all discussions on return hubs.

“On concrete cases, then we will have to see if this is compliant with the convention,” he said. He stressed that “all countries must be able to define their migration policy”.

Officials involved in setting up the migration centres expect legal challenges, but say the scheme is grounded in human rights law.

Rights organisations say the scheme is bound to fail. “Member states may call them ‘return hubs’ or even ‘welcome centres’, but no euphemism can hide the violence of uprooting people from the life they’ve been building in Europe, and sending them to a country they don’t even know, without family, networks or meaningful prospects,” said Chiara Catelli of Picum, a pan-European organisation that campaigns for the rights of undocumented migrants.

world.title: US basketball player arrested with 75lb of marijuana at Nigerian airport, say authorities
world.snippet: Suspect named as Greene Da’monte Khiree Drug smuggling carries life sentence in Nigeria An American basketball player has been arrested i...
world.content:
An American basketball player has been arrested in Nigeria for allegedly attempting to smuggle 33.95kg (75lb) of marijuana into the country.

Nigeria’s National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLEA) said a 28-year-old player named as Greene Da’monte Khiree from the state of Georgia was arrested at Lagos’s main airport last Wednesday after he arrived on a flight from Thailand via the United Arab Emirates.

The NDLEA said the player told them he had come to Nigeria to “build networks” for his basketball career. The agency said evidence on his phone suggested he had “knowledge of and involvement in the drug trafficking activity”. The NDLEA said it detained the player when he attempted to leave the airport with his hand luggage after abandoning two checked-in bags. The agency said those two bags were found to contain 32 parcels of marijuana, and a tracking device.

Nigeria has strict drug laws, and trafficking carries a sentence of life in prison.

A basketball player by the name of Damonte Greene is listed on the roster of the Pattani Raptors in the Thai Premier Men’s League. Greene, a Georgia native, played college basketball for Reinhardt University and South Georgia Technical College. He played semi-professional basketball in the US before representing a number of teams in Thailand.

WNBA star Brittney Griner and former Utah State player Jarred Shaw were imprisoned in Russia and Indonesia respectively for marijuana offenses. Griner was released in December 2022, while Shaw remains in prison.

world.title: Relocation of Cape Town baboons to sanctuary ignites heated protests
world.snippet: Demonstrators tried to block vehicle carrying the baboons, whose capture authorities say is needed to protect both primate and human The ...
world.content:
The relocation of a troop of baboons in Cape Town to a wildlife sanctuary has triggered furious protests by local people opposed to their capture, which officials argue is necessary to stop human-wildlife conflict in the city.

The 44-member Waterfall troop (named after the area they mainly inhabit) was captured in the southern seaside suburb of Simon’s Town on Friday and Saturday. A second, smaller Seaforth troop is also due to be moved.

The growth in both baboon and human populations in Cape Town in recent years has led to increased conflict and more baboons dying as a result. Meanwhile, a heated debate has raged between people who believe that baboons and humans can coexist and those who argue that baboons in urban areas are in danger and in some cases need to be relocated. Some animal rights activists have compared authorities’ baboon management to apartheid.

During Friday’s relocation, outraged protesters tried to stop vehicles taking the baboons away. One person sprayed a fire extinguisher, according to the Daily Maverick, a local news outlet.

After the confrontation, the local Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals branch urged those opposed to the baboons’ capture not to try to stop the vehicles. “Capture and transport are already stressful for the baboons,” it said in a statement. “Delaying their arrival prolongs their time in crates and risks adding to that stress – this is not fair on the baboons.”

It said it remained opposed to the baboon’s relocation, adding: “Our presence did not imply support … our inspectors are present because the animals need someone looking out for them.”

On Sunday, dozens of people sat outside the wildlife centre in a silent protest, some tying flowers to the fence. Baboons from a different troop also gathered at the boundary, calling to the newly captive animals, the Daily Maverick reported.

“We stand together for the Seaforth and Waterfall troops, for their freedom, their dignity and their right to live as wild animals,” Mandy Neal, the administrator of the Save Kogelfontein Baboons Facebook group, posted on Monday, calling for weekly Sunday silent protests. “ Our message is simple: CAPTIVITY IS NOT CONSERVATION.”

The City of Cape Town said in a statement on Sunday that the relocation had been successful, with the baboons being monitored 24/7 after being checked by vets and the females receiving contraceptive implants.

It said: “The Waterfall troop has been relocated due to the severity and persistence of human-baboon conflict in the Simon’s Town urban environment, the limited available natural low-lying habitat, the increasing risk to the baboons’ welfare, and public safety concerns … [and] as a very last resort after other interventions were evaluated and deemed ineffective, and as an alternative to culling.”

Prof Justin O’Riain, a behavioural ecologist at the University of Cape Town, said the baboon management plan had undergone two years of public consultations. “It has thus been disappointing watching members of the public and select NGOs, many which did not engage in the stakeholder process, now compromising the safety and welfare of the baboons and people through violent actions directed at staff and baboons in transit.”

world.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
world.snippet: After a month-long investigation it was concluded that Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which won the £10,000 Caine prize, was ‘human-...
world.content:
The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.

Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”

She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.

Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.

Associated Press contributed to this report

world.title: Lewis Hamilton visits Egypt’s Rafah crossing and Gaza aid facilities
world.snippet: Seven-time F1 world champion tours border area and logistics warehouses operated by Egyptian Red Crescent Lewis Hamilton has visited Egyp...
world.content:
Lewis Hamilton has visited Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with the Gaza Strip to meet organisations sending humanitarian aid to the territory.

The seven-time Formula One world champion has spoken out about conflict and humanitarian crises in the region, and has called for peace. He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire.

“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine. I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage,” Hamilton said in October.

A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

Israeli forces have continued to advance, expanding their control from 53% of the territory to at least 60%, an independent commission of UN experts said last month.

Airstrikes also continue, and Israeli fire along the advancing front has killed at least 196 Palestinians, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls, the commission said.

Hamilton toured Egypt’s Rafah border crossing with Gaza before visiting logistics warehouses operated by the Egyptian Red Crescent, which facilitates the entry of aid to Gaza.

At the crossing, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you.” He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Khaled Megawer, the governor of North Sinai, where Rafah is located, said the visit was intended to help Hamilton learn about Egypt’s efforts to send aid to Gaza.

The visit comes after Hamilton made his 400th race start on Sunday at the São Paulo Grand Prix at Interlagos.

The first black F1 driver, he made his debut with McLaren in 2007. He is only the second F1 driver to start 400 races after his former teammate Fernando Alonso, who achieved the milestone in 2024.
